titulo.texto: Monument 13: the ruler in the mouth of the earth

frase_gancho.texto: A seated figure in the open mouth of the earth.

puente_narrativo.texto: Continue along your route: the slope has another scene with the mouth of the earth.

guion_corto.texto: A person seated inside the open mouth of the earth. That is how some sources describe Monument Thirteen: a figure seated in the mouth of an earth being, surrounded by vegetation. Less than half of the relief survives, and it sits under an INAH roof. It is compared with Monument One, El Rey, who also sits in a cave. Even though more than half is missing, the scene can still be recognized. In both cases, the cave seems to be a doorway into the earth. It is not an isolated case: Monument Nine in the museum shows a mouth with open jaws. The three pieces share the idea of the mouth of the earth.

guion_largo.texto:
Some pieces arrive almost complete. Others do not. Of Monument Thirteen, less than half survives, and even so it tells us a great deal.

The sources we consulted, Mesoweb and The Post Hole, describe it as a person seated in the open mouth of an earth monster, with vegetation. Today it sits under a roof built by INAH. We were not able to consult a more complete academic source, so this description remains open to correction.

It should be looked at alongside two other monuments. The first is [Monument One](chz_17_monumento_1_el_rey), El Rey. Grove describes it as a richly attired person seated in a C-shaped cave, which is the mouth of a supernatural creature. The second is [Monument Nine](chz_02_museo_portal_inframundo), the Portal to the Underworld, a mouth with open jaws.

The three speak of the same thing from different angles: the mouth of the earth as an entrance. Arqueología Mexicana gathers the idea that the mountain is the place where ancestors and supernatural beings dwell, and that the cave is the access to that home.

With that key, a figure seated in a stone mouth is not simply in a place. It is on the threshold between two worlds. We do not know whether it was a ruler, an ancestor or a ritual figure. The sources do not say, and that is why we speak of a figure.

It is also a lesson in reading. An incomplete relief is still a source. What is missing is compared with what survives in other monuments, and from that contrast the hypothesis emerges.

There is a useful difference with the woman of [Monument Twenty-One](chz_09_monumento_21_mujer). She stands on the face of a supernatural earth being. This figure, by contrast, is seated inside the mouth. In one case the person treads on the earth; in the other, enters it.

As for its date, this relief belongs to the same world as the other reliefs of the hill. Grove points out that almost all the monuments of Chalcatzingo were sculpted around seven hundred to five hundred years before Christ.

The roof that covers it serves a practical purpose. Grove warns in the PARI Journal about the damage that acid rain does to the reliefs, and INAH has built roofs and walls to protect them.

In the art of this period one speaks of an earth monster: a supernatural creature whose open mouth works as a cave. The sources consulted use that expression for this monument.

Mesoweb and The Post Hole are specialized popular-interest sites. They are useful for locating the relief and describing it, but it is best to check them against an academic study. An incomplete scene invites questions, and that too is part of visiting an archaeological site. Look at the relief slowly and compare what is missing with what survives.

If you come from the terraces, you will notice the change of atmosphere. Here the art speaks of places where the world opens.
